title: Conjugations
description: Every verb and adjective form a conversation needs, with tables built by rule and how often each is heard, plus the grammar patterns that attach to them.

conventions.romaji: kotoba's stored spelling: modified Hepburn, lowercase, no macrons, long vowels as spelled (sou, daijoubu, kirei), wa/o/e particles, っ before ch = t (kotchi). Leading hyphen = attaches to a word.
conventions.register: romaji = casual form, learned first; polite = desu/masu counterpart, or null when there is no register difference.
conventions.freqRank: rank in jiten.moe drama frequency list (CC BY-SA 4.0); freqNote explains tokenizer-split forms. null = no usable rank.
conventions.contrastGroup: items sharing a group name are learned side by side; their examples share a base sentence.

blocks.label: How verbs work
blocks.rationale: The machinery every form below uses: which group a verb is in, how its stem shifts, the te/ta sound changes, and the few exceptions.
blocks.interference: Godan lookalikes like kaeru and hairu get treated as ichidan (kaeta, haita instead of kaetta, haitta).

items.english: Every verb is in one of three groups, and the group decides how it changes.
items.use: Check a new verb's group once; every form follows from it.
items.ja: 一段・五段・する・来る
items.kana: いちだん・ごだん・する・くる

example.romaji: gohan tabete, sugu kaetta yo
example.ja: ご飯食べて、すぐ帰ったよ。
example.english: I ate and went straight home.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan o tabete, sugu kaerimashita
examplePolite.ja: ご飯を食べて、すぐ帰りました。
examplePolite.english: I ate and went straight home.

items.notes: Lookalikes: kaeru (go home), hairu, shiru, hashiru, iru (need) and kiru (cut) end in -iru/-eru but are godan: kaetta, haitta, shitte. Kiru (wear) and iru (be) are ichidan.
items.name: verb groups
items.formation: Ichidan verbs end in -iru or -eru and just drop ru (taberu → tabe-). Godan verbs change their last syllable (kau → kawanai, kaimasu). Only suru and kuru are irregular.

items.english: Godan verbs shift their last vowel to a, i, e or o to fit the ending.
items.use: Know which ending takes which vowel and you can build most forms of any godan verb.
items.ja: 書か・書き・書け・書こ
items.kana: かか・かき・かけ・かこ

example.romaji: ima wa kawanai kedo, raigetsu kaou kana
example.ja: 今は買わないけど、来月買おうかな。
example.english: I'm not buying it now, but maybe next month.

examplePolite.romaji: ima wa kaimasen ga, raigetsu kaou to omoimasu
examplePolite.ja: 今は買いませんが、来月買おうと思います。
examplePolite.english: I won't buy it now, but I think I'll buy it next month.

items.notes: Verbs ending in a vowel plus u take wa before -nai: kau → kawanai, iu → iwanai (not kaanai).
items.name: the four stems
items.formation: Godan: a before -nai (kakanai), i before -masu and -tai (kakimasu), e before -ba and can-do (kakeba, kakeru), o plus u for let's (kakou). Ichidan just drops ru and adds the ending (tabenai, tabemasu). Watch the sounds: a final u becomes wa (kawanai), tsu becomes chi (machimasu), su becomes shi (hanashimasu).

items.english: Godan verbs change sound before -te and -ta, depending on their last syllable.
items.use: -te, -ta, -tara and -teru all share these changes, so drilling them once pays off everywhere.

example.romaji: eki made aruite, densha ni notta
example.ja: 駅まで歩いて、電車に乗った。
example.english: I walked to the station and got on the train.

examplePolite.romaji: eki made aruite, densha ni norimashita
examplePolite.ja: 駅まで歩いて、電車に乗りました。
examplePolite.english: I walked to the station and got on the train.

items.notes: iku → itte, not iite. Some forms sound the same: itte can come from iku (go) or iu (say), katte from kau (buy) or katsu (win).
items.name: te/ta sound changes
items.formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add te (tabete). Godan: u/tsu/ru → tte, mu/bu/nu → nde, ku → ite, gu → ide, su → shite. Exceptions: iku → itte, suru → shite, kuru → kite; -ta works the same way.

items.english: The few verbs (plus the adjective ii) that break the patterns.
items.use: They are among the most common words in speech, so their odd forms come up constantly.
items.ja: する・来る・行く・ある・いい
items.kana: する・くる・いく・ある・いい

example.romaji: jikan nai kara, kyou wa konai tte
example.ja: 時間ないから、今日は来ないって。
example.english: He says he has no time, so he's not coming today.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga nai node, kyou wa konai sou desu
examplePolite.ja: 時間がないので、今日は来ないそうです。
examplePolite.english: Apparently he has no time, so he isn't coming today.

items.notes: There is no aranai or kuranai: aru → nai, kuru → konai.
items.name: the exceptions
items.formation: suru → shinai, shite, dekiru (can); kuru → konai, kite, korareru (can). iku → itte, itta; aru → nai; ii → yokunai, yokatta. Honorifics irassharu, kudasaru, ossharu and nasaru take -aimasu: irasshaimasu, kudasaimasu.

blocks.label: Now and not
blocks.rationale: Present and negative in both registers: the four forms behind most sentences.
blocks.interference: Plain and polite pairs blur together; aranai for nai, and -u verbs losing their w (kaanai for kawanai).

items.english: Plain present and future: I do, I will do.
items.use: The everyday verb form with friends and family. It also goes before a noun to describe it: taberu mono (things to eat).

example.romaji: ashita nan ji ni kuru?
example.ja: 明日何時に来る？
example.english: What time are you coming tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita nan ji ni kimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日何時に来ますか？
examplePolite.english: What time are you coming tomorrow?

items.notes: There's no separate future tense: taberu covers both 'I eat' and 'I'll eat'. For 'I'm eating now', use -te iru.
items.name: dictionary form
items.formation: It's the form you find in the dictionary, so nothing changes. Every verb ends in u: ichidan in -iru/-eru, godan in u, ku, gu, su, tsu, nu, bu, mu or ru; plus suru and kuru.

items.english: Polite present and future: I do, I will do.
items.use: With strangers, staff, colleagues and anyone you'd call -san. The safe default while you're learning.

example.romaji: kono densha wa shibuya ni ikimasu ka?
example.ja: この電車は渋谷に行きますか？
example.english: Does this train go to Shibuya?

items.notes: The final u is nearly silent: tabemasu sounds like 'tabemas'.
items.name: polite present
items.formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add masu (tabemasu). Godan: change the last u to i, add masu (kaimasu, machimasu, hanashimasu). suru → shimasu, kuru → kimasu.

items.english: Plain negative: I don't, I won't.
items.use: The everyday 'don't / won't' with friends and family. -nai desu is a softer polite option.

example.romaji: kyou wa ikanai. chotto tsukareta
example.ja: 今日は行かない。ちょっと疲れた。
example.english: I'm not going today. I'm a bit tired.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ikimasen. chotto tsukaremashita
examplePolite.ja: 今日は行きません。ちょっと疲れました。
examplePolite.english: I'm not going today. I'm a bit tired.

items.notes: With a rising tone, ikanai? is an invitation (want to go?), not just a question.
items.name: plain negative
items.formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add nai (tabenai). Godan: change the last u to a, add nai (kakanai, matanai); a final u becomes wa (kawanai). suru → shinai, kuru → konai, aru → nai.

items.english: Polite negative: I don't, I won't.
items.use: Politely saying you don't or won't do something, including polite refusals.

example.romaji: sumimasen, osake wa nomimasen
example.ja: すみません、お酒は飲みません。
example.english: Sorry, I don't drink alcohol.

items.notes: In everyday polite talk -nai desu (tabenai desu) is also common and sounds a little softer.
items.name: polite negative
items.formation: Swap -masu for -masen: tabemasen, kaimasen, machimasen. suru → shimasen, kuru → kimasen.

blocks.label: The past
blocks.rationale: The same four slots moved into the past, plain and polite.
blocks.interference: -nakatta used for 'not yet' where mada -tenai belongs; dropped sound changes (kaeta for kaetta).

items.english: Plain past: I did.
items.use: Casually telling what happened; with mou it means 'already' (mou tabeta).

example.romaji: kinou, ano eiga mita?
example.ja: 昨日、あの映画見た？
example.english: Did you see that movie yesterday?

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, ano eiga o mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、あの映画を見ましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you see that movie yesterday?

items.notes: -ta also marks a discovery right now: a, atta! means 'oh, here it is!', not 'it was here'.
items.name: plain past
items.formation: Same sound changes as -te, with a instead of e: tabeta, katta, nonda, kaita, oyoida, hanashita. iku → itta, suru → shita, kuru → kita.

items.english: Polite past: I did.
items.use: Telling what happened to people you speak politely to. Set phrases too: wakarimashita (understood), arigatou gozaimashita.

example.romaji: shuumatsu wa tomodachi to umi ni ikimashita
example.ja: 週末は友達と海に行きました。
example.english: I went to the beach with friends at the weekend.

items.notes: The i is nearly silent: tabemashita sounds like 'tabemashta'.
items.name: polite past
items.formation: Swap -masu for -mashita: tabemashita, kaimashita, ikimashita. suru → shimashita, kuru → kimashita.

items.english: Plain negative past: I didn't.
items.use: Casually saying something didn't happen.

example.romaji: kesa wa nani mo tabenakatta
example.ja: 今朝は何も食べなかった。
example.english: I didn't eat anything this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: kesa wa nani mo tabemasen deshita
examplePolite.ja: 今朝は何も食べませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I didn't eat anything this morning.

items.notes: For 'haven't done it yet', use mada -tenai (mada tabetenai), not mada tabenakatta.
items.name: plain negative past
items.formation: Make the -nai form, then swap nai for nakatta: tabenakatta, kawanakatta, ikanakatta. suru → shinakatta, kuru → konakatta.

items.english: Polite negative past: I didn't.
items.use: Politely saying something didn't happen, often in apologies: shirimasen deshita (I didn't know).

example.romaji: sumimasen, zenzen kizukimasen deshita
example.ja: すみません、全然気づきませんでした。
example.english: Sorry, I didn't notice at all.

items.notes: In conversation -nakatta desu (tabenakatta desu) is just as common and a little softer.
items.name: polite negative past
items.formation: Take -masen and add deshita: tabemasen deshita, kaimasen deshita. suru → shimasen deshita, kuru → kimasen deshita.

blocks.label: The te-form
blocks.rationale: The te-form and the requests built on it: do it, please do it, please don't.
blocks.interference: -naide (please don't) confused with -nakute; bare -te heard as unfinished rather than as a request.

items.english: Links actions (and then), gives a reason, or on its own asks someone to do something.
items.use: Everywhere: chaining what you did, explaining why, and casual requests like chotto matte.

example.romaji: chotto matte, sugu iku kara
example.ja: ちょっと待って、すぐ行くから。
example.english: Hang on, I'll be right there.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto matte kudasai, sugu ikimasu
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと待ってください、すぐ行きます。
examplePolite.english: Just a moment, please. I'll be right there.

items.notes: The tense comes from the last verb: okite, gohan tabete, dekaketa = I got up, ate and left.
items.name: te-form
items.formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add te (tabete). Godan: u/tsu/ru → tte, mu/bu/nu → nde, ku → ite, gu → ide, su → shite. iku → itte, suru → shite, kuru → kite.

items.english: Please do...
items.use: Asking politely, for example to staff or strangers, and in instructions.

example.romaji: sumimasen, mou ichido itte kudasai
example.ja: すみません、もう一度言ってください。
example.english: Sorry, please say that again.

items.notes: kudasai still sounds like an instruction; to ask a favour, -te kuremasen ka or -te moraemasen ka is softer.
items.name: polite request
items.formation: te-form plus kudasai: tabete kudasai, matte kudasai, nonde kudasai. suru → shite kudasai, kuru → kite kudasai.

items.english: Don't...; also 'without doing'.
items.use: Asking someone not to do something: -naide with friends, -naide kudasai politely. Also 'without': nani mo tabenaide deta (left without eating).

example.romaji: shinpai shinaide. daijoubu da kara
example.ja: 心配しないで。大丈夫だから。
example.english: Don't worry. I'm fine.

examplePolite.romaji: shinpai shinaide kudasai. daijoubu desu kara
examplePolite.ja: 心配しないでください。大丈夫ですから。
examplePolite.english: Please don't worry. I'm fine.

items.notes: 'Please don't' is -naide, not -nakute: tabenaide (don't eat it).
items.name: please don't
items.formation: Make the -nai form and add de: tabenaide, kawanaide, ikanaide. suru → shinaide, kuru → konaide. Add kudasai to make it polite.

blocks.label: Deciding and arranging
blocks.rationale: Say what you decided, what got decided for you, and what you were told to do.
blocks.interference: koto ni suru (you chose) vs koto ni naru (it was decided or turned out that way).

items.english: it's been decided that; end up doing
items.use: For plans settled by others or by circumstance; the past, -koto ni natta, is the usual way to announce news.

example.romaji: raigetsu oosaka ni tenkin suru koto ni natta yo
example.ja: 来月大阪に転勤することになったよ
example.english: I'm being transferred to Osaka next month.

examplePolite.romaji: raigetsu oosaka ni tenkin suru koto ni narimashita
examplePolite.ja: 来月大阪に転勤することになりました
examplePolite.english: I'll be transferring to Osaka next month.

items.notes: Compare -koto ni suru, where you made the choice yourself. -koto ni natte iru states a rule or standing arrangement.
items.formation: dictionary form or -nai form + koto ni naru

items.english: decide to
items.use: Usually past, -koto ni shita, to report a choice you made; -koto ni shite iru means it's your habit or rule.

example.romaji: ashita kara hashiru koto ni shita
example.ja: 明日から走ることにした
example.english: I've decided to start running tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita kara hashiru koto ni shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 明日から走ることにしました
examplePolite.english: I've decided to start running tomorrow.

items.notes: Compare -koto ni naru (decided for you). To choose an item, use noun + ni suru: 'koohii ni suru'.
items.formation: dictionary form or -nai form + koto ni suru

items.english: tell someone to; ask someone to
items.use: Reports an instruction indirectly; put the verb in -nai form for 'told not to'.

example.romaji: isha ni sake o yameru you ni iwareta
example.ja: 医者に酒をやめるように言われた
example.english: The doctor told me to quit drinking.

examplePolite.romaji: isha ni osake o yameru you ni iwaremashita
examplePolite.ja: 医者にお酒をやめるように言われました
examplePolite.english: My doctor told me to stop drinking.

items.notes: Most often passive: -you ni iwareta, 'I was told to'. To pass on a message: '-you ni tsutaete' (tell them to).
items.formation: dictionary form or -nai form + you ni iu (also tanomu, tsutaeru)

items.english: make a point of; try to (as a habit)
items.use: For an ongoing effort, not a one-off attempt; -you ni shite iru means 'I make sure to'.

example.romaji: yoru wa amai mono tabenai you ni shiteru
example.ja: 夜は甘い物食べないようにしてる
example.english: I try not to eat sweets at night.

examplePolite.romaji: yoru wa amai mono o tabenai you ni shite imasu
examplePolite.ja: 夜は甘い物を食べないようにしています
examplePolite.english: I make a point of not eating sweets at night.

items.notes: Don't mix with -you ni naru (come to be able to) or -ou to suru (try once).
items.formation: dictionary form or -nai form + you ni suru

blocks.label: Credit and blame
blocks.rationale: Say what helped, what's to blame, and excuse yourself.
blocks.interference: okage de is for good results, no sei de for bad ones.

items.english: thanks to
items.use: For a good result; the helper comes first.

example.romaji: kimi no okage de maniatta yo
example.ja: 君のおかげで間に合ったよ
example.english: Thanks to you, I made it in time.

examplePolite.romaji: minasan no okage de maniaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 皆さんのおかげで間に合いました
examplePolite.english: Thanks to all of you, we made it in time.

items.notes: 'okage sama de' is the set reply to 'how are you / how did it go?': 'fine, thanks'. For a bad result use no sei de.
items.formation: noun + no okage de; plain-form clause + okage de

items.english: because of (blaming)
items.use: For a bad result, pinning it on the cause.

example.romaji: kaze no sei de zenzen nemurenakatta
example.ja: 風邪のせいで全然眠れなかった
example.english: I couldn't sleep at all because of this cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze no sei de zenzen nemuremasen deshita
examplePolite.ja: 風邪のせいで全然眠れませんでした
examplePolite.english: I couldn't sleep at all because of my cold.

items.notes: 'X no sei da' means 'it's X's fault': 'watashi no sei?' (is it my fault?). Compare okage de for good results.
items.formation: noun + no sei de; plain-form clause + sei de

items.english: blame it on
items.use: The person or thing blamed goes before no sei; often a complaint about unfair blame.

example.romaji: nandemo hito no sei ni suru na yo
example.ja: 何でも人のせいにするなよ
example.english: Don't blame everything on other people.

examplePolite.romaji: nandemo hito no sei ni shinaide kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 何でも人のせいにしないでください
examplePolite.english: Please don't blame everything on others.

items.notes: 'watashi no sei ni shinaide' = don't put it on me. Pairs with no sei de, 'because of'.
items.formation: noun + no sei ni suru

items.english: because, you see (giving an excuse)
items.use: Explains why something went wrong, usually your own slip, in a soft, apologetic way.

example.romaji: kyuu ni ame ga futte kita mon dakara, okurechatta
example.ja: 急に雨が降ってきたもんだから、遅れちゃった
example.english: It suddenly started raining, so I ended up late.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni ame ga futte kita mono desu kara, okurete shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 急に雨が降ってきたものですから、遅れてしまいました
examplePolite.english: It suddenly started raining, so I'm afraid I was late.

items.notes: Also mon de: 'isogashikatta mon de'. It sounds like an excuse, so use -kara or -node for a neutral reason.
items.formation: plain form + mon dakara (noun or na-adjective + na mon dakara)

items.english: precisely because; it's because ... that
items.use: Stresses that this reason is the real point, often turning a seeming drawback into the reason.

example.romaji: taisetsu da kara koso, hakkiri iu n da yo
example.ja: 大切だからこそ、はっきり言うんだよ
example.english: It's precisely because you matter that I'm being blunt.

examplePolite.romaji: taisetsu da kara koso, hakkiri iu n desu
examplePolite.ja: 大切だからこそ、はっきり言うんです
examplePolite.english: It's precisely because you matter to me that I'm being frank.

items.notes: Compare kara tte, 'just because ... doesn't mean'. Koso alone stresses the word before it: 'kochira koso' (likewise, the pleasure's mine).
items.formation: plain form + kara koso

blocks.label: Ongoing and done
blocks.rationale: te-form plus iru: what's going on, what was going on, and what hasn't happened yet.
blocks.interference: -teru as a resulting state (kekkon shiteru, kiteru) heard as an action in progress; shittenai for shiranai.

items.english: Is doing, or is in a state (is married, knows, lives somewhere).
items.use: What someone is doing right now, ongoing habits, and states like shitteru (know) and kekkon shiteru (married). -teru is how it sounds in speech.

example.romaji: nee, ima nani shiteru no?
example.ja: ねえ、今何してるの？
example.english: Hey, what are you doing right now?

examplePolite.romaji: ima nani o shite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今何をしていますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you doing right now?

items.notes: With change verbs it's the result, not the action: kekkon shiteru = is married, kiteru = has come (is here).
items.name: ongoing or state
items.formation: te-form plus iru; in speech the i drops: tabeteru, matteru, nonderu. suru → shiteru, kuru → kiteru.

items.english: Was doing, or had been in a state.
items.use: Setting the scene in a story (what you were doing when...), and past states like 'I used to live in...'.

example.romaji: gomen, sakki made zutto neteta
example.ja: ごめん、さっきまでずっと寝てた。
example.english: Sorry, I was asleep until just now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sakki made zutto nete imashita
examplePolite.ja: すみません、さっきまでずっと寝ていました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I was asleep until just now.

items.notes: shitteta means 'I knew'; 'I didn't know' is shiranakatta, not shittenakatta.
items.name: was doing
items.formation: te-form plus ita; in speech the i drops: tabeteta, matteta, nondeta. suru → shiteta, kuru → kiteta.

items.english: Isn't doing; or hasn't done (yet).
items.use: With mada, it's how you say you haven't done something yet.

example.romaji: mada hirugohan tabetenai n da yo
example.ja: まだ昼ご飯食べてないんだよ。
example.english: I haven't had lunch yet.

examplePolite.romaji: mada hirugohan o tabete imasen
examplePolite.ja: まだ昼ご飯を食べていません。
examplePolite.english: I haven't had lunch yet.

items.notes: 'Not yet' is mada -tenai, not -nakatta. And 'I don't know' is shiranai, not shittenai.
items.name: not doing, not yet
items.formation: te-form plus inai; in speech the i drops: tabetenai, mattenai, nondenai. suru → shitenai, kuru → kitenai.

blocks.label: Wanting and inviting
blocks.rationale: Wants, suggestions and invitations, from casual to polite.
blocks.interference: -mashou (assumes yes) vs -masen ka (leaves room to refuse); kaerou (let's go home) vs kaeru.

items.english: Want to do.
items.use: Saying what you want to do, or asking a friend what they want to do.

example.romaji: nanka amai mono tabetai na
example.ja: なんか甘いもの食べたいな。
example.english: I kind of want something sweet.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika amai mono ga tabetai desu
examplePolite.ja: 何か甘いものが食べたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like something sweet.

items.notes: Use it for yourself or to ask the listener; for someone else, say -tagatteru (kodomo ga asobitagatteru).
items.name: want to
items.formation: Take the -masu stem and add tai: tabetai, kaitai, machitai, nomitai. suru → shitai, kuru → kitai. It then bends like an i-adjective: -takunai (don't want to), -takatta (wanted to).

items.english: Let's...; with to omou, I think I'll...
items.use: Casual suggestions to friends (ikou!), and plans: -ou to omotteru (I'm thinking of...).

example.romaji: mou osoi shi, sorosoro kaerou ka
example.ja: もう遅いし、そろそろ帰ろうか。
example.english: It's late. Shall we head home?

examplePolite.romaji: mou osoi node, sorosoro kaerimashou ka
examplePolite.ja: もう遅いので、そろそろ帰りましょうか。
examplePolite.english: It's getting late. Shall we head home?

items.notes: Hold the long vowel: kaerou (let's go home) vs kaeru (go home).
items.name: let's (casual)
items.formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add you (tabeyou, miyou). Godan: change the last u to o and add u (kaou, matou, nomou, ikou). suru → shiyou, kuru → koyou.

items.english: Let's...; with ka, shall we...? or shall I...?
items.use: Polite suggestions, and offers of help: mochimashou ka? (shall I carry it?).

example.romaji: sono nimotsu, omoi deshou? mochimashou ka
example.ja: その荷物、重いでしょう？持ちましょうか。
example.english: That bag looks heavy. Shall I carry it?

items.notes: To invite someone, -masen ka is softer; -mashou assumes they'll say yes.
items.name: let's / shall I (polite)
items.formation: Swap -masu for -mashou: tabemashou, ikimashou. suru → shimashou, kuru → kimashou. Add ka to offer or suggest more softly.

items.english: Won't you...? Would you like to...?
items.use: Inviting someone politely while leaving them room to say no.

example.romaji: kondo, issho ni gohan tabemasen ka?
example.ja: 今度、一緒にご飯食べませんか？
example.english: Would you like to get a meal together sometime?

items.notes: Despite the negative, it's an invitation. The casual version is -nai? with a rising tone (ikanai?).
items.name: polite invitation
items.formation: -masen plus ka: tabemasen ka, ikimasen ka. suru → shimasen ka, kuru → kimasen ka.

blocks.label: Adjectives and the copula
blocks.rationale: The core shapes of adjectives and nouns: is, was, isn't, wasn't, probably. i-adjectives change their own ending; na-adjectives and nouns lean on da, desu and deshou.
blocks.interference: Polite past is -katta desu, not -i deshita; ii becomes yo- in every changed form (yokatta, yokunai); da never follows an i-adjective.

items.english: Says something is X, casually or politely.
items.use: The base of every description. Casually an i-adjective stands alone (takai!) and da is often dropped (kirei!); politely add desu.

example.romaji: kono mise, chotto takai ne
example.ja: この店、ちょっと高いね
example.english: This place is a bit pricey, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kono omise wa chotto takai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: このお店はちょっと高いですね
examplePolite.english: This shop is a little expensive, isn't it.

items.notes: Never put da after an i-adjective (takai da ✗); casually just say takai.
items.name: adjective plain and polite
items.formation: i-adjectives: plain as is (takai, ii), polite + desu (takai desu, ii desu). Na-adjectives and nouns: plain + da (kirei da, gakusei da), polite + desu (kirei desu, gakusei desu).

items.english: Was X.
items.use: Saying how something was: oishikatta, tanoshikatta. yokatta on its own also means 'I'm glad' or 'what a relief'.

example.romaji: kinou no raamen, mecha oishikatta
example.ja: 昨日のラーメン、めちゃおいしかった
example.english: Yesterday's ramen was so good.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no raamen, totemo oishikatta desu
examplePolite.ja: 昨日のラーメン、とてもおいしかったです
examplePolite.english: The ramen yesterday was very good.

items.notes: Polite past is -katta desu, not -i deshita (takai deshita ✗).
items.name: adjective past
items.formation: i-adjectives: drop -i, add -katta (takakatta); ii → yokatta. Na-adjectives and nouns: + datta (kirei datta, gakusei datta). Polite: -katta desu, or deshita after na-adjectives and nouns.

items.english: Is not X.
items.use: Everyday 'not': samukunai?, amari suki ja nai. Often softened with sonna ni or amari.

example.romaji: sonna ni takakunai yo, daijoubu
example.ja: そんなに高くないよ、大丈夫
example.english: It's not that expensive, it's fine.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni takakunai desu yo, daijoubu desu
examplePolite.ja: そんなに高くないですよ、大丈夫です
examplePolite.english: It's not that expensive. It's fine.

items.notes: ja nai? with a rising tone means 'isn't it?' (ii ja nai? = that's great, isn't it?), not 'it isn't'.
items.name: adjective negative
items.formation: i-adjectives: drop -i, add -kunai (takakunai); ii → yokunai. Na-adjectives and nouns: + ja nai (kirei ja nai, gakusei ja nai). Polite: -kunai desu, ja nai desu or ja arimasen.

items.english: Was not X.
items.use: Saying something wasn't so: anmari oishikunakatta. Usually softened with anmari or sonna ni.

example.romaji: eiga, anmari omoshirokunakatta
example.ja: 映画、あんまり面白くなかった
example.english: The movie wasn't all that good.

examplePolite.romaji: eiga wa amari omoshirokunakatta desu
examplePolite.ja: 映画はあまり面白くなかったです
examplePolite.english: The movie wasn't very interesting.

items.notes: ii changes to yo- here too: yokunakatta, never iikunakatta.
items.name: adjective negative past
items.formation: i-adjectives: drop -i, add -kunakatta (takakunakatta); ii → yokunakatta. Na-adjectives and nouns: + ja nakatta (kirei ja nakatta, gakusei ja nakatta).

items.english: Probably; or, said rising, 'right?'.
items.use: Guessing (ashita wa ame deshou) and checking that you agree (ii deshou?). Casual speech shortens it to desho and daro.

example.romaji: kore, kawaii desho? kinou katta n da
example.ja: これ、かわいいでしょ?昨日買ったんだ
example.english: Cute, right? I bought it yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, kawaii deshou? kinou katta n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: これ、かわいいでしょう?昨日買ったんですよ
examplePolite.english: Isn't this cute? I bought it yesterday.

items.notes: Rising deshou? asks you to agree; falling deshou is a guess. darou is mostly male or written; most people say desho casually.
items.name: probably / right?
items.formation: Plain form + deshou or darou: takai deshou, ii deshou. Na-adjectives and nouns drop da: kirei deshou, gakusei deshou.

blocks.label: Adjectives that link and change
blocks.rationale: What adjectives do inside a longer sentence: link (-kute / de), change (-ku naru), sit before a noun (na / no), set a condition (-kattara), and say how things look (-sou).
blocks.interference: -ku naru (becomes) vs -ku suru (makes it); stem + sou (looks) vs plain + sou da (I hear); ii → yokute, yoku, yosasou.

items.english: Links descriptions (X and Y), or gives a reason.
items.use: Stringing descriptions: yasukute oishii (cheap and tasty). Also a reason: samukute nerenakatta (too cold to sleep).

example.romaji: ano mise, yasukute oishii yo
example.ja: あの店、安くておいしいよ
example.english: That place is cheap and tasty.

examplePolite.romaji: ano omise wa yasukute oishii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: あのお店は安くておいしいですよ
examplePolite.english: That restaurant is cheap and good.

items.notes: Don't join adjectives with to (yasui to oishii ✗); to only joins nouns.
items.name: adjective te-form
items.formation: i-adjectives: drop -i, add -kute (takakute); ii → yokute. Na-adjectives and nouns: + de (kirei de, gakusei de). Verbs link with their te-form, as in the table (tabete, itte).

items.english: Becomes X; the -ku / ni part is also the adverb form.
items.use: For changes: samuku natta, jouzu ni natta. The same -ku / ni form works as an adverb: hayaku, kirei ni.

example.romaji: kyuu ni samuku natta ne
example.ja: 急に寒くなったね
example.english: It suddenly got cold, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni samuku narimashita ne
examplePolite.ja: 急に寒くなりましたね
examplePolite.english: It's suddenly turned cold, hasn't it.

items.notes: naru is for things that change; suru is for changing something yourself (heya o kirei ni suru = tidy the room).
items.name: becoming (-ku naru)
items.formation: i-adjectives: drop -i, add -ku (takaku naru); ii → yoku naru. Na-adjectives and nouns: + ni (kirei ni naru, gakusei ni naru).

items.english: Describes a noun directly: an X thing.
items.use: Constantly, to describe things and people: takai mise, kirei na hito, gakusei no toki.

example.romaji: kinou, sugoku kirei na hito mita
example.ja: 昨日、すごくきれいな人見た
example.english: I saw a really good-looking person yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, totemo kirei na hito o mimashita
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、とてもきれいな人を見ました
examplePolite.english: Yesterday I saw a very beautiful person.

items.notes: Some words end in -ei or -i but take na: kirei na, yuumei na, not kirei hito.
items.name: before a noun
items.formation: i-adjectives go straight before the noun (takai hon, ii hito). Na-adjectives add na (kirei na hito). Nouns add no (gakusei no toki).

items.english: If it's X.
items.use: Conditions about qualities: takakattara kawanai. yokattara (if you like) is a very common polite offer.

example.romaji: takakattara, betsu no mise ni shiyou
example.ja: 高かったら、別の店にしよう
example.english: If it's expensive, let's go somewhere else.

examplePolite.romaji: takakattara, betsu no omise ni shimashou
examplePolite.ja: 高かったら、別のお店にしましょう
examplePolite.english: If it's expensive, let's try another place.

items.notes: yokattara is less 'if it's good' than 'if you'd like' (yokattara douzo = please, help yourself).
items.name: adjective if
items.formation: i-adjectives: drop -i, add -kattara or -kereba (takakattara, takakereba); ii → yokattara, yokereba. Na-adjectives and nouns: + nara or dattara (kirei nara, gakusei dattara). Verbs use -tara, as in the table (tabetara, ittara).

items.english: Looks X, judging by appearance.
items.use: Reacting to what you see: oishisou! (looks good!), tanoshisou, genki sou.

example.romaji: waa, kore mecha oishisou!
example.ja: わあ、これめちゃおいしそう!
example.english: Wow, this looks so good!

examplePolite.romaji: waa, totemo oishisou desu ne
examplePolite.ja: わあ、とてもおいしそうですね
examplePolite.english: Oh, that looks delicious.

items.notes: kawaisou means 'poor thing', not 'looks cute'. And plain form + sou da is hearsay: takai sou da = I hear it's expensive.
items.name: looks (adjective)
items.formation: i-adjectives: drop -i, add sou (oishisou); ii → yosasou, nai → nasasou. Na-adjectives: + sou (genki sou). Verbs use the -masu stem, as in the table (tabesou, furisou).

blocks.label: Pretending and trying
blocks.rationale: Talk about pretending, attempts that got cut off, and what you won't do.
blocks.interference: -ou to suru (tried, was about to) vs -te goran and -te miru (try it and see).

items.english: pretend to; act as if
items.use: Speech often drops the o: 'shiranai furi suru'.

example.romaji: kanojo, kikoenai furi shiteta yo
example.ja: 彼女、聞こえないふりしてたよ
example.english: She was pretending not to hear.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo wa kikoenai furi o shite imashita
examplePolite.ja: 彼女は聞こえないふりをしていました
examplePolite.english: She was pretending not to hear.

items.notes: Also written フリ. The everyday ones are 'shiranai furi' (playing dumb) and 'neta furi' (pretending to sleep).
items.formation: plain form + furi o suru; noun + no furi; na-adjective + na furi

items.english: try to; be about to
items.use: Mostly past, -ou to shita, for an attempt that failed or got interrupted: 'I was just about to'.

example.romaji: neyou to shitara, tomodachi kara denwa ga kita
example.ja: 寝ようとしたら、友達から電話が来た
example.english: Just as I was going to sleep, a friend called.

examplePolite.romaji: neyou to shitara, tomodachi kara denwa ga kimashita
examplePolite.ja: 寝ようとしたら、友達から電話が来ました
examplePolite.english: Just as I was about to go to sleep, a friend called.

items.notes: Compare -te miru (try it and see) and -ou to omou (plan to). Negative: 'kikou to shinai' (won't even listen).
items.formation: volitional form (-ou / -you) + to suru

items.english: have no intention of; don't feel like
items.use: A firm 'I'm not going to'.

example.romaji: mou ano mise ni iku ki wa nai yo
example.ja: もうあの店に行く気はないよ
example.english: I've got no intention of going to that place again.

examplePolite.romaji: mou ano mise ni iku ki wa arimasen
examplePolite.ja: もうあの店に行く気はありません
examplePolite.english: I have no intention of going to that shop again.

items.notes: The positive is -ki ga aru (be willing): 'yaru ki aru?' (are you up for it?). 'yaru ki' alone means motivation.
items.formation: dictionary form + ki wa nai

items.english: try doing (said to a child or junior)
items.use: A gentle 'go on, try it' from parents, teachers or seniors.

example.romaji: chotto tabete goran, oishii yo
example.ja: ちょっと食べてごらん、おいしいよ
example.english: Go on, have a taste, it's good.

items.notes: Never use it upward; to equals say -te mite. 'goran kudasai' is the polite 'please look' in shops and announcements.
items.formation: -te form + goran

blocks.label: Can, must and needn't
blocks.rationale: Fuller ways to say what's allowed, possible, pointless, out of the question or right.
blocks.interference: koto wa nai (no need) vs -ta koto wa nai (never have); wake ni wa ikanai vs wake ja nai.

items.english: must not; not allowed to
items.use: The fuller, firmer version of -cha dame; heard in rules, warnings and from parents and teachers.

example.romaji: koko de shashin totcha ikenai n da yo
example.ja: ここで写真撮っちゃいけないんだよ
example.english: You're not allowed to take photos here.

examplePolite.romaji: koko de shashin o totte wa ikemasen
examplePolite.ja: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません
examplePolite.english: Photography is not permitted here.

items.notes: -nakya ikenai / -nakereba ikenai means 'must'. On its own, 'ikenai!' means 'oh no' or 'oops, that's bad'.
items.formation: -te form + wa ikenai (spoken -cha ikenai)

items.english: can; be able to
items.use: A fuller, more formal way to say the potential form; common in rules, signs and polite explanations.

example.romaji: kono apuri de yoyaku suru koto mo dekiru yo
example.ja: このアプリで予約することもできるよ
example.english: You can also book with this app.

examplePolite.romaji: kono apuri de yoyaku suru koto mo dekimasu
examplePolite.ja: このアプリで予約することもできます
examplePolite.english: You can also make a booking with this app.

items.notes: Everyday speech usually prefers the potential form (taberareru, yomeru); -koto mo dekiru, 'can also', is where it sounds most natural.
items.formation: dictionary form + koto ga dekiru

items.english: there's no need to
items.use: Reassures someone or tells them not to bother: 'you don't have to go that far'.

example.romaji: sonna ni ayamaru koto nai yo
example.ja: そんなに謝ることないよ
example.english: There's no need to apologize so much.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni ayamaru koto wa arimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: そんなに謝ることはありませんよ
examplePolite.english: There's no need to apologize like that.

items.notes: Speech often drops wa. Don't mix with -ta koto wa nai, 'have never'.
items.formation: dictionary form + koto wa nai

items.english: can't very well; can't just
items.use: Something is possible but wrong for social or moral reasons: 'I can't just leave him there'.

example.romaji: kyou wa kaisha yasumu wake ni wa ikanai n da
example.ja: 今日は会社休むわけにはいかないんだ
example.english: I can't very well skip work today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kaisha o yasumu wake ni wa ikanai n desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日は会社を休むわけにはいかないんです
examplePolite.english: I really can't take today off work.

items.notes: After -nai it means 'have no choice but to': 'ikanai wake ni wa ikanai' (I can't not go). Don't mix with wake ja nai (it's not that).
items.formation: dictionary form + wake ni wa ikanai; -nai form + wake ni wa ikanai = have to

items.english: should; ought to
items.use: A strong, principled 'should'; for friendly advice -ta hou ga ii sounds softer.

example.romaji: sore wa saki ni iu beki datta yo
example.ja: それは先に言うべきだったよ
example.english: You should have said that first.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa saki ni iu beki deshita ne
examplePolite.ja: それは先に言うべきでしたね
examplePolite.english: You should have mentioned that first.

items.notes: -beki datta = should have; -beki ja nai = shouldn't.
items.formation: dictionary form + beki (suru often becomes subeki)

blocks.label: When it happens
blocks.rationale: Say how often, since when, and at what moment something happened.
blocks.interference: -ru koto ga aru (sometimes) vs -ta koto ga aru (have ever).

items.english: sometimes does; there are times when
items.use: Says something happens now and then; often with tama ni or tokidoki.

example.romaji: tama ni asagohan nuku koto aru yo
example.ja: たまに朝ご飯抜くことあるよ
example.english: I skip breakfast now and then.

examplePolite.romaji: tama ni asagohan o nuku koto ga arimasu
examplePolite.ja: たまに朝ご飯を抜くことがあります
examplePolite.english: I sometimes skip breakfast.

items.notes: Don't mix with -ta koto ga aru, 'have done before'; only the verb form tells them apart.
items.formation: dictionary form or -nai form + koto ga aru

items.english: every time; whenever
items.use: The second thing happens without fail on each occasion.

example.romaji: kono uta kiku tabi ni naichau
example.ja: この歌聞くたびに泣いちゃう
example.english: I cry every time I hear this song.

examplePolite.romaji: kono uta o kiku tabi ni naite shimaimasu
examplePolite.ja: この歌を聞くたびに泣いてしまいます
examplePolite.english: I cry every time I hear this song.

items.notes: Close to -to itsumo; tabi ni stresses each single time.
items.formation: dictionary form + tabi ni; noun + no tabi ni

items.english: since; ever since
items.use: From a past event until now, usually with something that has stayed true.

example.romaji: sotsugyou shite irai, zenzen atte nai ne
example.ja: 卒業して以来、全然会ってないね
example.english: We haven't seen each other at all since graduation.

examplePolite.romaji: sotsugyou shite irai, zenzen atte imasen ne
examplePolite.ja: 卒業して以来、全然会っていませんね
examplePolite.english: We haven't met at all since we graduated.

items.notes: Sounds a bit formal; casual talk often says -te kara zutto. 'sore irai' = ever since then.
items.formation: -te form + irai; noun + irai

items.english: just when I thought; no sooner ... than
items.use: Something unexpected follows right away, or the reality turns out different: 'I thought X, but'.

example.romaji: yatto hareta to omottara, mata ame da
example.ja: やっと晴れたと思ったら、また雨だ
example.english: Just when it finally cleared up, it's raining again.

examplePolite.romaji: yatto hareta to omottara, mata ame desu ne
examplePolite.ja: やっと晴れたと思ったら、また雨ですね
examplePolite.english: Just as it cleared up, it's raining again.

items.notes: It can also be a plain 'if you think': 'takai to omottara, kawanakute ii yo'. Context tells them apart.
items.formation: plain form (often -ta) + to omottara

items.english: in the middle of; right while
items.use: Usually for an interruption that came at a bad moment.

example.romaji: kaigi no saichuu ni onaka ga natchatta
example.ja: 会議の最中にお腹が鳴っちゃった
example.english: My stomach growled right in the middle of the meeting.

examplePolite.romaji: kaigi no saichuu ni onaka ga natte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 会議の最中にお腹が鳴ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: My stomach rumbled in the middle of the meeting.

items.notes: Stronger than -te iru aida (while). 'ima saichuu' = I'm right in the middle of it.
items.formation: -te iru form + saichuu ni; noun + no saichuu ni

items.english: the moment that; as soon as
items.use: The second thing happens instantly and usually unexpectedly.

example.romaji: suwatta totan ni nechatta
example.ja: 座った途端に寝ちゃった
example.english: He fell asleep the second he sat down.

examplePolite.romaji: suwatta totan ni nete shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 座った途端に寝てしまいました
examplePolite.english: He fell asleep the moment he sat down.

items.notes: Not for your own plans: 'as soon as I get home, I'll call' is -tara sugu.
items.formation: -ta form + totan (ni)

blocks.label: Very polite speech
blocks.rationale: Understand and use the keigo of shops, offices and polite requests.
blocks.interference: kudasaru (they kindly do it for you) vs itadaku (you humbly receive it).

items.english: is; there is, we have (very polite)
items.use: Shop and hotel staff use it in place of desu and arimasu; you mostly hear it rather than say it.

example.romaji: kochira ga atarashii moderu de gozaimasu
example.ja: こちらが新しいモデルでございます
example.english: This is the new model.

items.notes: The dictionary form gozaru is archaic. You do say it in set phrases: arigatou gozaimasu, ohayou gozaimasu, omedetou gozaimasu.
items.formation: noun + de gozaimasu (= desu); noun + ga gozaimasu (= arimasu)

items.english: could you (kindly)
items.use: The standard polite request to strangers, staff and people at work; -te itadakemasen ka is softer still.

example.romaji: sumimasen, shashin totte itadakemasu ka
example.ja: すみません、写真撮っていただけますか
example.english: Excuse me, could you take our photo?

items.notes: One step politer than -te moraemasu ka. Literally 'can I receive the favour of you doing'.
items.formation: -te form + itadakemasu ka / itadakemasen ka

items.english: kindly do (for me), said of someone above you
items.use: The respectful -te kureru: a teacher, boss or customer does something for you.

example.romaji: sensei ga eki made okutte kudasatta n da
example.ja: 先生が駅まで送ってくださったんだ
example.english: My teacher kindly took me to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: sensei ga eki made okutte kudasaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 先生が駅まで送ってくださいました
examplePolite.english: My teacher was kind enough to take me to the station.

items.notes: Common in thanks: 'kite kudasatte arigatou gozaimasu' (thank you for coming). -te kudasai is its request form; never use it for your own actions.
items.formation: -te form + kudasaru (masu form: kudasaimasu)

items.english: humbly do; allow me to
items.use: Announces your own action very politely, as if asking permission; everywhere in business, shops and speeches.

example.romaji: kyou wa kore de shitsurei sasete itadakimasu
example.ja: 今日はこれで失礼させていただきます
example.english: If you'll excuse me, I'll be leaving now.

items.notes: Overused in business talk, so it can sound stiff. With friends, just say -sasete or -sasete morau.
items.formation: causative -te form + itadaku (yasumasete, ikasete, shitsurei sasete)

blocks.label: Quoting and referring
blocks.rationale: Ask whether, pass on what you heard, sum it up, and refer back to what was said.
blocks.interference: to ieba (speaking of X) vs sou ieba (that reminds me).

items.english: whether or not
items.use: Tucks a yes/no question into a sentence, usually before wakaranai, kiku or shiraberu.

example.romaji: kare ga kuru ka dou ka wakannai
example.ja: 彼が来るかどうかわかんない
example.english: I don't know whether he's coming.

examplePolite.romaji: kare ga kuru ka dou ka wakarimasen
examplePolite.ja: 彼が来るかどうかわかりません
examplePolite.english: I don't know if he's coming or not.

items.notes: With a question word, use plain ka: 'itsu kuru ka wakaranai'.
items.formation: plain form + ka dou ka (noun or na-adjective drops da)

items.english: just as; the way (said, planned, shown)
items.use: Something matches what was said or shown; iu toori, 'just as you say', is the most common.

example.romaji: iwareta toori ni yatta kedo, dame datta
example.ja: 言われたとおりにやったけど、ダメだった
example.english: I did exactly what I was told, but it didn't work.

examplePolite.romaji: iwareta toori ni yarimashita ga, dame deshita
examplePolite.ja: 言われたとおりにやりましたが、ダメでした
examplePolite.english: I did it exactly as instructed, but it didn't work.

items.notes: 'sono toori' = exactly, that's right. 'yotei doori' = as planned.
items.formation: dictionary or -ta form + toori; noun + no toori; noun + doori

items.english: speaking of; when you think of
items.use: Picks up a word just said to shift topic, or names the classic example: 'kyouto to ieba otera'.

example.romaji: natsu to ieba, yappari suika da yo ne
example.ja: 夏といえば、やっぱりスイカだよね
example.english: When you think summer, it's got to be watermelon.

examplePolite.romaji: natsu to ieba, yappari suika desu yo ne
examplePolite.ja: 夏といえば、やっぱりスイカですよね
examplePolite.english: Speaking of summer, watermelon is the classic, isn't it?

items.notes: Sou ieba is the stand-alone 'that reminds me'. Casual: 'X tte ieba'.
items.formation: noun or plain form + to ieba

items.english: it means that; I hear that
items.use: Sums up or draws a conclusion ('so that means...'), or passes on news you heard.

example.romaji: jaa, kyanseru to iu koto da ne
example.ja: じゃあ、キャンセルということだね
example.english: So that means it's cancelled.

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, kyanseru to iu koto desu ne
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、キャンセルということですね
examplePolite.english: So it's cancelled, then.

items.notes: Casual speech says tte koto: 'kyanseru tte koto?'. On the news, '... to iu koto desu' means 'reportedly'.
items.formation: plain form + to iu koto da

items.english: according to
items.use: Names the source of what you heard; the sentence usually ends in -sou da, rashii or tte.

example.romaji: tenki yohou ni yoru to, ashita wa yuki rashii yo
example.ja: 天気予報によると、明日は雪らしいよ
example.english: According to the forecast, it's going to snow tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: tenki yohou ni yoru to, ashita wa yuki da sou desu
examplePolite.ja: 天気予報によると、明日は雪だそうです
examplePolite.english: According to the weather forecast, it'll snow tomorrow.

items.notes: Not the same as -ni yoru, 'it depends on'. -ni yoreba means the same and sounds more formal.
items.formation: noun + ni yoru to

blocks.label: If and when
blocks.rationale: The four conditionals; -tara covers most needs and the others add shades.
blocks.interference: All four translate as 'if': -to can't be followed by a request, nara looks ahead, -tara means once it's happened.

items.english: If..., or when (once)..., then something happens.
items.use: The everyday 'if' and 'when (once)': the conditional to reach for first.

example.romaji: eki ni tsuitara, renraku shite
example.ja: 駅に着いたら、連絡して。
example.english: Let me know when you get to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki ni tsuitara, renraku shite kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 駅に着いたら、連絡してください。
examplePolite.english: Please let me know when you get to the station.

items.notes: On its own with a rising tone it's advice: yasundara? = why don't you take a break?
items.name: if / when
items.formation: Make the -ta form and add ra: tabetara, kattara, nondara, ittara. suru → shitara, kuru → kitara.

items.english: If... (a general condition).
items.use: Conditions and advice; -ba ii means 'you just have to' or 'you should'.

example.romaji: sensei ni kikeba ii yo
example.ja: 先生に聞けばいいよ。
example.english: You should just ask the teacher.

examplePolite.romaji: sensei ni kikeba ii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 先生に聞けばいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You can just ask the teacher.

items.notes: For a one-off 'when / after', -tara is more natural; keep -ba for conditions and -ba ii advice.
items.name: if (condition)
items.formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add reba (tabereba, mireba). Godan: change the last u to e, add ba (kaeba, nomeba, ikeba). suru → sureba, kuru → kureba.

items.english: Whenever or if X happens, Y follows naturally.
items.use: Directions, how things work, and habits: migi ni magaru to... (turn right and...).

example.romaji: kono botan osu to, denki tsuku yo
example.ja: このボタン押すと、電気つくよ。
example.english: Press this button and the light comes on.

examplePolite.romaji: kono botan o osu to, denki ga tsukimasu
examplePolite.ja: このボタンを押すと、電気がつきます。
examplePolite.english: If you press this button, the light comes on.

items.notes: No requests or plans after it: say tsuitara renraku shite, not tsuku to renraku shite.
items.name: whenever / if (automatic)
items.formation: Dictionary form plus to: taberu to, kau to, iku to. suru → suru to, kuru → kuru to. For the negative, -nai to.

items.english: If that's the case; if you're going to...
items.use: Reacting to what someone just said, often with advice.

example.romaji: kyouto iku nara, kasa motte itte
example.ja: 京都行くなら、傘持っていって。
example.english: If you're going to Kyoto, take an umbrella.

examplePolite.romaji: kyouto ni iku nara, kasa o motte itte kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 京都に行くなら、傘を持っていってください。
examplePolite.english: If you're going to Kyoto, please take an umbrella.

items.notes: nara looks ahead: iku nara = if you're going (advice before you go); ittara = once you've gone.
items.name: if that's the case
items.formation: Dictionary form plus nara: taberu nara, kau nara, iku nara. suru → suru nara, kuru → kuru nara. It also follows nouns and the -nai form.

blocks.label: Must and don't have to
blocks.rationale: Obligation, permission and prohibition, mostly built from -nai and -te.
blocks.interference: -nakya (have to) vs -nakute mo ii (don't have to); -cha dame (mustn't) vs -chau (did it).

items.english: Have to, must.
items.use: Casual -nakya (or -nakucha) for what you've got to do. The full -nakereba naranai is formal.

example.romaji: yabai, mou ikanakya. mata ne
example.ja: やばい、もう行かなきゃ。またね。
example.english: Yikes, I've got to go. See you.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, mou ikanakereba narimasen
examplePolite.ja: すみません、もう行かなければなりません。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I have to go now.

items.notes: Don't mix it up with -nakute mo ii: ikanakya = I have to go; ikanakute mo ii = I don't have to go.
items.name: have to
items.formation: Make the -nai form, then swap nai for nakya (or nakereba): tabenakya, kawanakya, ikanakya. suru → shinakya, kuru → konakya. The 'or else' ending (ikenai, naranai) is usually dropped in speech.

items.english: Not ... and; because (it's) not ...; with mo ii, don't have to.
items.use: Giving a reason something didn't work out, and with mo ii, telling someone they don't need to.

example.romaji: kyou wa konakute mo ii yo
example.ja: 今日は来なくてもいいよ。
example.english: You don't have to come today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa konakute mo ii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 今日は来なくてもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to come today.

items.notes: For 'please don't', use -naide, not -nakute: tabenaide (don't eat it).
items.name: not, and / don't have to
items.formation: Make the -nai form, then swap nai for nakute: tabenakute, kawanakute, ikanakute. suru → shinakute, kuru → konakute.

items.english: It's OK to...; can I...?
items.use: Asking for permission (-te mo ii?) and giving it.

example.romaji: kore, tabete mo ii?
example.ja: これ、食べてもいい？
example.english: Can I eat this?

examplePolite.romaji: kore, tabete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これ、食べてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: May I eat this?

items.notes: In speech mo often drops: tabete ii? = can I eat it?
items.name: may / it's OK to
items.formation: te-form plus mo ii: tabete mo ii, katte mo ii, nonde mo ii. suru → shite mo ii, kuru → kite mo ii.

items.english: Mustn't, don't.
items.use: Casual 'you can't do that', often to children or close friends.

example.romaji: koko de shashin totcha dame da yo
example.ja: ここで写真撮っちゃだめだよ。
example.english: You can't take photos here.

examplePolite.romaji: koko de shashin o totte wa ikemasen
examplePolite.ja: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。
examplePolite.english: You mustn't take photos here.

items.notes: Don't confuse it with -chau (did, often by accident): tabechatta = I ate it all; tabecha dame = don't eat it.
items.name: mustn't
items.formation: It's -te wa squeezed together: -te → -cha, -de → -ja, then add dame: tabecha dame, katcha dame, nonja dame. suru → shicha dame, kuru → kicha dame.

blocks.label: Helper verbs after -te
blocks.rationale: Each is the te-form plus a small verb or particle: -te shimau, -te oku, -te miru, -te mo. Two of them shrink in speech (-chau, -toku), so the full and short forms are learned together.
blocks.interference: -toku (do ahead) vs -teku (-te iku); -chau (end up) vs -cha (-te wa, must not); -te mo (even if) vs -te miru (try).

items.english: Did it completely, or did it by accident and regret it.
items.use: All over casual talk, mostly in the past: tabechatta (I ate it all), wasurechatta (oops, I forgot). The full -te shimau is for more careful speech.

example.romaji: a, kasa densha ni wasurechatta
example.ja: あ、傘電車に忘れちゃった
example.english: Oh no, I left my umbrella on the train.

examplePolite.romaji: kasa o densha ni wasurete shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 傘を電車に忘れてしまいました
examplePolite.english: I left my umbrella on the train.

items.notes: -chatta is past (did it, oops); -chau is now or about to (I'll end up doing it).
items.name: end up / finish (-chau)
items.formation: Take the te-form: -te becomes -chau, -de becomes -jau (tabechau, katchau, nonjau). suru → shichau, kuru → kichau. Past: -chatta / -jatta.

items.english: Do it now, ready for later; or leave it as it is.
items.use: Planning and getting things ready: yoyaku shitoku ne (I'll book it). Also 'leave it': hottoite (leave me alone).

example.romaji: mise, yoyaku shitoku ne
example.ja: 店、予約しとくね
example.english: I'll book the restaurant.

examplePolite.romaji: omise o yoyaku shite okimasu ne
examplePolite.ja: お店を予約しておきますね
examplePolite.english: I'll book the restaurant ahead of time.

items.notes: -toku (do ahead) sounds close to -teku (-te iku, do before going): shitoku = I'll do it now for later; shiteku = I'll do it on my way.
items.name: do ahead (-toku)
items.formation: Take the te-form: -te oku becomes -toku, -de oku becomes -doku (tabetoku, kattoku, nondoku). suru → shitoku, kuru → kitoku. Request: -toite / -doite.

items.english: Try doing it and see how it goes.
items.use: Suggesting or reporting a try: tabete mite (try it), itte mita (I went to check it out).

example.romaji: kore oishii yo, tabete mite
example.ja: これおいしいよ、食べてみて
example.english: This is good, try some.

examplePolite.romaji: kore oishii desu yo, tabete mite kudasai
examplePolite.ja: これおいしいですよ、食べてみてください
examplePolite.english: This is good, please try some.

items.notes: -te miru is 'try it and see'; -ou to suru is 'attempt it' (and maybe fail).
items.name: try doing
items.formation: te-form + miru: tabete miru, katte miru, nonde miru, shite miru, kite miru.

items.english: Even if / even though.
items.use: For 'even if' and 'no matter what': ame futtemo iku. Also the start of asking permission: -temo ii? (is it OK if I...?).

example.romaji: ame futtemo, ashita wa iku yo
example.ja: 雨降っても、明日は行くよ
example.english: Even if it rains, I'm going tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ame ga futtemo, ashita wa ikimasu
examplePolite.ja: 雨が降っても、明日は行きます
examplePolite.english: Even if it rains, I'll go tomorrow.

items.notes: After a verb, -demo is -te mo (nondemo = even if I drink), not the word demo 'but'.
items.name: even if
items.formation: te-form + mo: tabetemo, kattemo, nondemo, shitemo, kitemo.

blocks.label: Doing two things
blocks.rationale: Three ways to fit two actions in one sentence: as examples (-tari), at the same time (-nagara), or one without the other (-zu ni).
blocks.interference: Each takes a different stem: -tari the past (tabetari), -nagara the -masu stem (tabenagara), -zu ni the negative stem (tabezu ni). Mixing the stems is the usual slip.

items.english: Doing things like A and B, among other things.
items.use: Listing sample activities, usually closed with suru: eiga mitari, kaimono shitari shita. A single -tari keeps it vague (netari shiteta = I was sleeping and stuff).

example.romaji: shuumatsu wa eiga mitari, kaimono shitari shita
example.ja: 週末は映画見たり、買い物したりした
example.english: At the weekend I watched movies, went shopping, that kind of thing.

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa eiga o mitari, kaimono o shitari shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 週末は映画を見たり、買い物をしたりしました
examplePolite.english: At the weekend I watched movies and went shopping, among other things.

items.notes: -tari lists examples; -te strings actions in order (eiga mite, kaimono shita = watched a movie, then shopped).
items.name: things like (-tari)
items.formation: Past form + ri: tabetari, kattari, nondari, shitari, kitari. Close the list with suru (-tari -tari suru).

items.english: Doing one thing while doing another (same person).
items.use: Two actions at once by one person: arukinagara, terebi minagara. The main action comes last.

example.romaji: itsumo terebi minagara gohan tabeteru
example.ja: いつもテレビ見ながらご飯食べてる
example.english: I always eat while watching TV.

examplePolite.romaji: itsumo terebi o minagara gohan o tabemasu
examplePolite.ja: いつもテレビを見ながらご飯を食べます
examplePolite.english: I always eat while watching TV.

items.notes: Only for one person doing both. When someone else does the other thing, use -te iru aida (while they...).
items.name: while doing
items.formation: -masu stem + nagara. Ichidan: drop -ru (tabenagara). Godan: change the final -u to -i (nominagara, hanashinagara). suru → shinagara, kuru → kinagara.

items.english: Without doing it.
items.use: Doing one thing without the other: nani mo iwazu ni kaetta. In chat -naide is more common; -zu ni turns up in stories and set phrases (wasurezu ni).

example.romaji: nani mo iwazu ni kaetchatta
example.ja: 何も言わずに帰っちゃった
example.english: He went home without saying anything.

examplePolite.romaji: nani mo iwazu ni kaette shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 何も言わずに帰ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: He went home without saying a word.

items.notes: suru becomes sezu ni, not shizu ni. -naide means the same and is the everyday choice (tabenaide).
items.name: without doing
items.formation: Negative stem + zu ni. Ichidan: drop -ru (tabezu ni). Godan: change the final -u to -a (kawazu ni, ikazu ni). suru → sezu ni, kuru → kozu ni.

blocks.label: Seeming and sure
blocks.rationale: Say how sure you are, from 'seems' to 'must be' to 'not necessarily'.
blocks.interference: you da (formal 'seems') vs mitai (casual) vs -sou (looks).

items.english: like; such as; a kind of
items.use: Goes before a noun to compare or give an example; casual mitai na does the same job.

example.romaji: dokoka de atta you na ki ga suru
example.ja: どこかで会ったような気がする
example.english: I feel like I've met you somewhere.

examplePolite.romaji: dokoka de atta you na ki ga shimasu
examplePolite.ja: どこかで会ったような気がします
examplePolite.english: I have a feeling we've met somewhere.

items.notes: -you na ki ga suru, 'I have a feeling that', is its most common use in speech. Before a verb or adjective it becomes -you ni.
items.formation: noun + no you na + noun; plain form + you na + noun

items.english: it seems; it looks like
items.use: A judgment from what you see or know; more formal than mitai, so you hear it in polite speech and on the news.

example.romaji: dare mo inai you da ne
example.ja: 誰もいないようだね
example.english: Looks like nobody's here.

examplePolite.romaji: dare mo inai you desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 誰もいないようですね
examplePolite.english: It seems no one is here.

items.notes: Casual equivalent: mitai. Compare -sou (looks, from appearance) and rashii (I hear).
items.formation: plain form + you da; noun + no you da; na-adjective + na you da

items.english: not necessarily; not always
items.use: Pushes back on an assumption; often with kanarazu shimo or itsumo.

example.romaji: takai kara oishii to wa kagiranai yo
example.ja: 高いからおいしいとは限らないよ
example.english: Expensive doesn't necessarily mean tasty.

examplePolite.romaji: takai kara oishii to wa kagirimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: 高いからおいしいとは限りませんよ
examplePolite.english: Just because it's expensive doesn't mean it's good.

items.notes: Kagiru alone means 'nothing beats': 'natsu wa biiru ni kagiru' (nothing beats beer in summer).
items.formation: plain form + to wa kagiranai

items.english: must be; no doubt
items.use: A confident guess from evidence; stronger than hazu.

example.romaji: ano futari, tsukiatteru ni chigai nai yo
example.ja: あの二人、付き合ってるに違いないよ
example.english: Those two must be dating.

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari wa tsukiatte iru ni chigai arimasen
examplePolite.ja: あの二人は付き合っているに違いありません
examplePolite.english: Those two are surely going out.

items.notes: A little bookish; in chat 'kitto ... da yo' or '... ni kimatteru' (it's obviously) are more common.
items.formation: plain form + ni chigai nai (noun or na-adjective drops da)

blocks.label: Ifs and hopes
blocks.rationale: Suppose things, set conditions and limits, and hope out loud.
blocks.interference: -to ii (I hope) vs -tara ii (you should); sae areba (as long as) vs de sae (even).

items.english: if; supposing; if it's true that
items.use: For a pure hypothetical or something you just learned; often moshi ... to shitara.

example.romaji: moshi takarakuji atatta to shitara, nani suru?
example.ja: もし宝くじ当たったとしたら、何する？
example.english: Say you won the lottery, what would you do?

examplePolite.romaji: moshi takarakuji ni atatta to shitara, nani o shimasu ka
examplePolite.ja: もし宝くじに当たったとしたら、何をしますか
examplePolite.english: Supposing you won the lottery, what would you do?

items.notes: To sureba and to suru to mean the same. 'da to shitara' = if that's the case.
items.formation: plain form + to shitara

items.english: I hope; it would be good if
items.use: Mostly -to ii ne to wish someone well, or -to ii na for your own hope.

example.romaji: ashita hareru to ii ne
example.ja: 明日晴れるといいね
example.english: Hope it's sunny tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita hareru to ii desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 明日晴れるといいですね
examplePolite.english: I hope it's sunny tomorrow.

items.notes: Same idea as -tara ii na. As advice it means 'it's best to': 'kono kusuri nomu to ii yo'.
items.formation: dictionary or -nai form + to ii

items.english: as long as; as far as
items.use: Sets a condition or limit: 'as long as I'm here', 'as far as I know'.

example.romaji: watashi no shitteru kagiri, kare wa dokushin da yo
example.ja: 私の知ってる限り、彼は独身だよ
example.english: As far as I know, he's single.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi no shitte iru kagiri, kare wa dokushin desu
examplePolite.ja: 私の知っている限り、彼は独身です
examplePolite.english: As far as I know, he isn't married.

items.notes: 'dekiru kagiri' = as much as possible. 'kyou kagiri' = today only, on sale signs.
items.formation: dictionary, -nai or -te iru form + kagiri

items.english: depending on; as soon as
items.use: After a noun it means 'it's up to'; after a -masu stem, 'as soon as', a polite promise at work.

example.romaji: iku ka dou ka wa tenki shidai da ne
example.ja: 行くかどうかは天気次第だね
example.english: Whether we go depends on the weather.

examplePolite.romaji: iku ka dou ka wa tenki shidai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 行くかどうかは天気次第ですね
examplePolite.english: Whether we go will depend on the weather.

items.notes: 'anata shidai' = it's up to you. 'wakari shidai gorenraku shimasu' (I'll contact you as soon as I know) is a set business line.
items.formation: noun + shidai (da); -masu stem + shidai

items.english: as long as there's; all you need is
items.use: Says one thing is all it takes; the general shape is X sae + a -ba form, and areba is the common one.

example.romaji: sumaho sae areba daijoubu
example.ja: スマホさえあれば大丈夫
example.english: As long as I've got my phone, I'm fine.

examplePolite.romaji: sumaho sae areba daijoubu desu
examplePolite.ja: スマホさえあれば大丈夫です
examplePolite.english: As long as I have my phone, I'll be fine.

items.notes: 'kimi sae yokereba' = if it's okay with you. Don't mix with de sae, 'even'.
items.formation: noun + sae + -ba form (areba, ireba, yokereba)

blocks.label: Even though
blocks.rationale: Push back, complain, make allowances and play things down.
blocks.interference: ni shite wa (for a) vs ni shite mo (even allowing for); kuse ni vs the neutral -noni.

items.english: even though (critical); and yet
items.use: Criticises someone for acting against what they are or know; sounds accusing, so keep it out of polite talk.

example.romaji: nani mo shiranai kuse ni, erasou ni iu na yo
example.ja: 何も知らないくせに、偉そうに言うなよ
example.english: You don't know a thing, so quit acting like an expert.

items.notes: -noni is the neutral 'even though'. Ending a sentence on kuse ni is a jab: 'shiranai kuse ni' (like you'd know).
items.formation: plain form + kuse ni; noun + no kuse ni; na-adjective + na kuse ni

items.english: just because
items.use: Almost always followed by a negative or a complaint: 'just because X doesn't mean Y'.

example.romaji: yasui kara tte, kaisugi da yo
example.ja: 安いからって、買いすぎだよ
example.english: Just because it's cheap doesn't mean you buy that much.

examplePolite.romaji: yasui kara to itte, kaisugi desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 安いからといって、買いすぎですよ
examplePolite.english: Even if it's cheap, that's too much to buy.

items.notes: Kara to itte is the fuller, more polite form. Compare kara koso, 'precisely because'.
items.formation: plain form + kara tte

items.english: even if; even so; still
items.use: Grants one point, then adds a reservation: 'even allowing for that'.

example.romaji: isogashii ni shite mo, renraku gurai shite yo
example.ja: 忙しいにしても、連絡ぐらいしてよ
example.english: Even if you're busy, at least get in touch.

examplePolite.romaji: isogashii ni shite mo, renraku gurai shite kudasai yo
examplePolite.ja: 忙しいにしても、連絡ぐらいしてくださいよ
examplePolite.english: Busy or not, please at least let me know.

items.notes: 'sore ni shite mo' = even so, still: 'sore ni shite mo samui ne'. Compare -ni shite wa, 'for a'.
items.formation: noun or plain form + ni shite mo

items.english: for a; considering (it's)
items.use: Says something is surprising given what it is: 'pretty good for a beginner'.

example.romaji: shoshinsha ni shite wa umai ne
example.ja: 初心者にしてはうまいね
example.english: You're good for a beginner.

examplePolite.romaji: shoshinsha ni shite wa jouzu desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 初心者にしては上手ですね
examplePolite.english: You're very good for a beginner.

items.notes: The result always goes against what you'd expect. Don't mix with -ni shite mo, 'even if'.
items.formation: noun or plain form + ni shite wa

items.english: although; that said; though it's only
items.use: Plays down what you just said: 'I cook, though it's just simple stuff'.

example.romaji: ryokou to itte mo, ippaku dake da yo
example.ja: 旅行といっても、一泊だけだよ
example.english: It's a trip, but only one night.

examplePolite.romaji: ryokou to itte mo, ippaku dake desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 旅行といっても、一泊だけですよ
examplePolite.english: I say a trip, but it's only one night.

items.notes: Casual: 'tte itte mo'. 'nan to itte mo' = when all's said and done.
items.formation: noun or plain form + to itte mo

blocks.label: Even and let alone
blocks.rationale: Go one step further: far from, not only, rather, even.
blocks.interference: dokoro ka flips the expectation; dake de naku just adds to it.

items.english: far from; let alone
items.use: Rejects an expectation and goes further the other way: 'far from cheap, it cost double'.

example.romaji: yasumu dokoro ka, kyuujitsu mo shigoto da yo
example.ja: 休むどころか、休日も仕事だよ
example.english: Rest? I'm even working my days off.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumu dokoro ka, kyuujitsu mo shigoto desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 休むどころか、休日も仕事ですよ
examplePolite.english: Far from resting, I'm working even on my days off.

items.notes: 'sore dokoro ja nai' = there's no time for that right now. Compare dake de naku, a neutral 'not only'.
items.formation: noun or plain form + dokoro ka

items.english: not only ... but also
items.use: The second half usually has mo: 'not only X, Y too'.

example.romaji: ano mise, oishii dake ja nakute yasui n da yo
example.ja: あの店、おいしいだけじゃなくて安いんだよ
example.english: That place isn't just tasty, it's cheap too.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa oishii dake de naku, yasui n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: あの店はおいしいだけでなく、安いんですよ
examplePolite.english: That restaurant is not only good but cheap as well.

items.notes: Speech usually says dake ja nakute; dake de naku sounds formal or written.
items.formation: noun or plain form + dake de naku

items.english: rather than; or rather; more like
items.use: Corrects your own word choice: 'not so much X as Y'.

example.romaji: samui to iu yori, mou itai yo
example.ja: 寒いというより、もう痛いよ
example.english: It's not so much cold as painful.

examplePolite.romaji: samui to iu yori, mou itai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 寒いというより、もう痛いですね
examplePolite.english: It's less cold than actually painful.

items.notes: Casual: 'tte iu yori'. The stand-alone filler 'to iu ka' (or rather) is even more common.
items.formation: noun or plain form + to iu yori

items.english: even
items.use: Picks an extreme case to make the point: 'even the teacher couldn't'.

example.romaji: sensei de sae wakaranakatta n da yo
example.ja: 先生でさえわからなかったんだよ
example.english: Even the teacher didn't know.

examplePolite.romaji: sensei de sae wakarimasen deshita
examplePolite.ja: 先生でさえわかりませんでした
examplePolite.english: Even the teacher couldn't work it out.

items.notes: Casual talk usually says de mo: 'kodomo de mo wakaru'. Don't mix with sae ... -ba, 'as long as'.
items.formation: noun + de sae; after another particle, plain sae

blocks.label: Point of view
blocks.rationale: Say in what role, for whom, toward whom and about what.
blocks.interference: ni totte (from X's view) vs no tame ni (for X's benefit); -muke vs -muki.

items.english: as (a role); in the capacity of
items.use: Names the role, status or purpose: 'as a teacher', 'as a present'.

example.romaji: tomodachi to shite suki na dake da yo
example.ja: 友達として好きなだけだよ
example.english: I just like him as a friend.

examplePolite.romaji: tomodachi to shite suki na dake desu
examplePolite.ja: 友達として好きなだけです
examplePolite.english: I only like him as a friend.

items.notes: 'watashi to shite wa' = speaking for myself. Not the -te form of -ou to suru (try to).
items.formation: noun + to shite

items.english: for; to (from someone's point of view)
items.use: Says who something matters to or how it looks to them, not who benefits.

example.romaji: watashi ni totte, kazoku ga ichiban daiji
example.ja: 私にとって、家族が一番大事
example.english: For me, family matters most.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi ni totte, kazoku ga ichiban daiji desu
examplePolite.ja: 私にとって、家族が一番大事です
examplePolite.english: To me, family is the most important thing.

items.notes: For 'for your benefit' use no tame ni; for a gift just ni: 'kore, anata ni'.
items.formation: noun (person or group) + ni totte

items.english: toward; against; in contrast to
items.use: Marks who an attitude or action is aimed at: 'rude to customers', 'angry at him'.

example.romaji: kare, okyakusan ni taishite taido warui yo ne
example.ja: 彼、お客さんに対して態度悪いよね
example.english: He's got a bad attitude toward customers, hasn't he?

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa okyakusan ni taishite taido ga warui desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 彼はお客さんに対して態度が悪いですね
examplePolite.english: He's quite rude to customers, isn't he?

items.notes: Second use is contrast, 'whereas': 'ani ni taishite, otouto wa ...' (unlike his older brother, ...).
items.formation: noun + ni taishite; before a noun: ni taisuru

items.english: about; concerning; regarding
items.use: The formal ni tsuite, for meetings, emails and announcements.

example.romaji: sono ken ni kanshite wa, ato de gorenraku shimasu
example.ja: その件に関しては、後でご連絡します
example.english: I'll get back to you about that later.

items.notes: In casual talk say ni tsuite instead. Before nouns: 'kankyou ni kansuru nyuusu' (news about the environment).
items.formation: noun + ni kanshite; before a noun: ni kansuru

items.english: aimed at; made for
items.use: Says who a product or service is designed for: 'for kids', 'for beginners'.

example.romaji: kono anime, kodomo muke ja nai yo
example.ja: このアニメ、子供向けじゃないよ
example.english: This anime isn't for kids.

examplePolite.romaji: kono anime wa kodomo muke ja arimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: このアニメは子供向けじゃありませんよ
examplePolite.english: This anime isn't meant for children.

items.notes: Don't mix with -muki, 'suited to': shoshinsha muki means it happens to suit beginners, muke that it was made for them.
items.formation: noun + muke (no + noun); noun + muke ni

blocks.label: Noun add-ons
blocks.rationale: Small endings that make a noun a type, a whole, a without, or a game.
blocks.interference: -goto (and all) and -gokko (playing at) sound alike.

items.english: -type; -style; kind of
items.use: Labels a person, look or thing by its type: 'oshare kei' (the stylish type).

example.romaji: karai kei no tabemono, daisuki nan da
example.ja: 辛い系の食べ物、大好きなんだ
example.english: I love anything spicy.

examplePolite.romaji: karai kei no tabemono ga daisuki nan desu
examplePolite.ja: 辛い系の食べ物が大好きなんです
examplePolite.english: I really love spicy kinds of food.

items.notes: Standard, not slang, in rikei and bunkei (science and arts tracks). Like 'tte kanji', it keeps a label vague.
items.formation: noun or adjective + kei

items.english: and all, including; every (-goto ni)
items.use: Noun + goto keeps the whole thing together ('skin and all'); -goto ni means each or every.

example.romaji: kono budou, kawa goto taberareru yo
example.ja: このぶどう、皮ごと食べられるよ
example.english: You can eat these grapes skin and all.

examplePolite.romaji: kono budou wa kawa goto taberaremasu yo
examplePolite.ja: このぶどうは皮ごと食べられますよ
examplePolite.english: You can eat these grapes with the skin on.

items.notes: With ni it means 'every': 'ichi jikan goto ni' (every hour). 'marugoto' = whole, entirely.
items.formation: noun + goto; noun or counter + goto ni

items.english: without
items.use: Doing something without a thing; also nashi ni and, in speech, nashi ja.

example.romaji: koohii nashi ja ikite ikenai yo
example.ja: コーヒーなしじゃ生きていけないよ
example.english: I can't live without coffee.

examplePolite.romaji: koohii nashi de wa ikite ikemasen
examplePolite.ja: コーヒーなしでは生きていけません
examplePolite.english: I couldn't live without coffee.

items.notes: When ordering, 'X nashi de' = hold the X: 'wasabi nashi de onegai shimasu'. With verbs use -naide or -zu ni.
items.formation: noun + nashi de

items.english: playing at; make-believe
items.use: Children's pretend games, or an adult doing a mock version of something.

example.romaji: kodomotachi ga oishasan gokko shiteru yo
example.ja: 子供たちがお医者さんごっこしてるよ
example.english: The kids are playing doctors.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomotachi ga oishasan gokko o shite imasu yo
examplePolite.ja: 子供たちがお医者さんごっこをしていますよ
examplePolite.english: The children are playing doctors.

items.notes: Onigokko (tag) is the best-known one. Said of adults it mocks: 'kazoku gokko' (just playing house).
items.formation: noun + gokko (o suru)

blocks.label: Can, be done, make do
blocks.rationale: The four voice forms: can (potential), be done (passive), make or let (causative), be made to (causative-passive). They are all built the same way, a vowel change plus -reru or -seru, so they are easiest to tell apart side by side.
blocks.interference: Ichidan potential and passive are identical (taberareru, mirareru), and kuru gives korareru for both. -aseru (make do) and -areru (be done) differ by one sound, and -asareru stacks both.

items.english: Says someone can or can't do something.
items.use: The everyday way to say can and can't: nihongo hanaseru?, ashita ikeru?, mou taberarenai.

example.romaji: nihongo, chotto hanaseru yo
example.ja: 日本語、ちょっと話せるよ
example.english: I can speak a little Japanese.

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo ga sukoshi hanasemasu
examplePolite.ja: 日本語が少し話せます
examplePolite.english: I can speak a little Japanese.

items.notes: Ichidan potential sounds the same as the passive (taberareru, mirareru); context tells. kaeru 'can buy' also sounds like kaeru 'go home'.
items.name: potential (can do)
items.formation: Godan: change the final -u to -eru (kau → kaeru, iku → ikeru). Ichidan: drop -ru, add -rareru (taberareru); in speech often just -reru (tabereru). suru → dekiru, kuru → korareru.

items.english: Something is done to someone, often with a feeling of 'it happened to me'.
items.use: Mostly for things done to you, often unwelcome: okorareta (I got told off), ame ni furareta (I got caught in the rain). At work the same form is also a light honorific (nanji ni kaeraremasu ka).

example.romaji: kinou buchou ni okorareta
example.ja: 昨日部長に怒られた
example.english: I got chewed out by my boss yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou buchou ni okoraremashita
examplePolite.ja: 昨日部長に怒られました
examplePolite.english: I got scolded by my manager yesterday.

items.notes: The person who does it to you takes ni (buchou ni). Ichidan passive and potential sound the same: mirareru = 'be seen' or 'can see'.
items.name: passive
items.formation: Godan: change the final -u to -a and add -reru (kau → kawareru, matsu → matareru). Ichidan: drop -ru, add -rareru (taberareru). suru → sareru, kuru → korareru.

items.english: Makes or lets someone do something.
items.use: Heard most as -sasete or -sasete kudasai, 'let me': chotto kangaesasete (let me think). Also for a parent or boss making someone do something.

example.romaji: kondo wa watashi ni harawasete yo
example.ja: 今度は私に払わせてよ
example.english: Let me pay next time.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo wa watashi ni harawasete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 今度は私に払わせてください
examplePolite.english: Please let me pay next time.

items.notes: -sasete kudasai asks to do it yourself; -te kudasai asks the other person to do it (harawasete = let me pay, haratte = you pay).
items.name: causative (make / let)
items.formation: Godan: change the final -u to -a and add -seru (kau → kawaseru, matsu → mataseru). Ichidan: drop -ru, add -saseru (tabesaseru). suru → saseru, kuru → kosaseru; the table shows the -te form (-sasete).

items.english: Being made to do something you didn't want to.
items.use: For complaining about being forced or kept: nomasareta (they made me drink), matasareta (I was kept waiting).

example.romaji: kinou mo sanjikan matasareta yo
example.ja: 昨日も三時間待たされたよ
example.english: I got kept waiting three hours again yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou mo sanjikan matasaremashita
examplePolite.ja: 昨日も三時間待たされました
examplePolite.english: I was kept waiting three hours again yesterday.

items.notes: Listen for the extra -sa-: nomasareta = I was made to drink; nomareta = someone drank it (on me).
items.name: causative-passive (be made to)
items.formation: Godan: change the final -u to -a and add -sareru (kau → kawasareru, matsu → matasareru); verbs in -su use -saserareru (hanasaserareru). Ichidan: drop -ru, add -saserareru (tabesaserareru). suru → saserareru, kuru → kosaserareru.

blocks.label: Commands
