blocks.rationale: Ways to tell someone to do or not do something, from rough (ike, iku na) to parental (-nasai) to blunt but personal (-te kure). You mostly hear these; for your own requests, -te and -te kudasai do the job.
blocks.interference: The command ike sounds like the potential ikeru; ike (go!) and iku na (don't go!) are opposites built on the same verb. -nasai sounds soft but talks down.

items.english: A blunt order: do it!
items.use: Heard in anger, among rough-talking male friends, in sports cheering and on signs. Learners mostly need to recognise it; ganbare (go for it!) and chotto mate (hang on) are the friendly exceptions.

example.romaji: oi, hayaku shiro yo
example.ja: おい、早くしろよ
example.english: Hey, hurry up!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, hayaku shite kudasai
examplePolite.ja: すみません、早くしてください
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, please hurry.

items.notes: The command ike (go!) and the potential ikeru (can go) share the -e sound; the bare -e at the end is the order.
items.name: command form
items.formation: Godan: change the final -u to -e (kau → kae, iku → ike). Ichidan: drop -ru, add -ro (tabero, miro). suru → shiro, kuru → koi.

items.english: A blunt 'don't!'.
items.use: Strong bans: parents to small kids, rough friends, signs and warnings. In normal talk people say -naide (sawaranaide).

example.romaji: abunai! sore sawaru na!
example.ja: 危ない!それ触るな!
example.english: Careful! Don't touch that!

examplePolite.romaji: abunai desu kara, sawaranaide kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 危ないですから、触らないでください
examplePolite.english: It's dangerous, so please don't touch it.

items.notes: Only a bare verb + na is a ban; na after other words is the feeling particle (ii na = that's nice).
items.name: don't! (blunt)
items.formation: Dictionary form + na, for every verb: taberu na, iku na, suru na, kuru na.

items.english: A firm instruction, the way a parent or teacher gives it.
items.use: Parents to kids, teachers to students: hayaku nenasai, chanto tabenasai. It also lives in set phrases: gomennasai, okaerinasai, oyasuminasai.

example.romaji: mou osoi kara, hayaku nenasai
example.ja: もう遅いから、早く寝なさい
example.english: It's late, go to bed now.

examplePolite.romaji: mou osoi desu kara, hayaku nete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: もう遅いですから、早く寝てください
examplePolite.english: It's late, so please go to bed.

items.notes: It sounds gentle but talks down; don't use it to adults you don't know.
items.name: -nasai command
items.formation: Use the -masu stem + nasai. Ichidan: drop -ru (tabenasai). Godan: change the final -u to -i (kainasai, machinasai, hanashinasai). suru → shinasai, kuru → kinasai.

items.english: Do it (for me): a blunt request.
items.use: Mostly men, to friends or juniors, or in tense moments: matte kure! Everyday requests use just -te (matte) or -te kureru? (matte kureru?).

example.romaji: chotto matte kure, sugu iku kara
example.ja: ちょっと待ってくれ、すぐ行くから
example.english: Hang on, I'll be right there.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto matte kudasai, sugu ikimasu kara
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと待ってください、すぐ行きますから
examplePolite.english: Just a moment, please. I'll be right there.

items.notes: -te kure is an order; -te kureru? is a friendly question. Same verb, very different tone.
items.name: blunt request
items.formation: te-form + kure: tabete kure, matte kure, nonde kure, shite kure, kite kure.

blocks.label: Looks, too much, easy
blocks.rationale: All three hang off the -masu stem: tabesou, tabesugiru, tabeyasui. One stem, three common add-ons.
blocks.interference: Stem + sou (looks like) vs dictionary form + sou da (I hear); -yasui (easy to) vs yasui (cheap).

items.english: Looks like it's about to happen.
items.use: Judging from what you see: ame furisou (looks like rain), nakisou (about to cry), ochisou (about to fall).

example.romaji: sora kurai ne, ame furisou
example.ja: 空暗いね、雨降りそう
example.english: The sky's dark. Looks like rain.

examplePolite.romaji: ame ga furisou desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 雨が降りそうですね
examplePolite.english: It looks like it's going to rain.

items.notes: Stem + sou = 'looks like'; dictionary form + sou da = 'I hear' (furu sou da = I hear it'll rain).
items.name: looks about to
items.formation: -masu stem + sou. Ichidan: drop -ru (tabesou). Godan: change the final -u to -i (furisou, nomisou). suru → shisou, kuru → kisou.

items.english: Doing something too much.
items.use: Mostly in the past, about overdoing it: tabesugita, nomisugita. Works on adjectives too: takasugiru (too expensive).

example.romaji: kinou nomisugite, atama itai
example.ja: 昨日飲みすぎて、頭痛い
example.english: I drank too much yesterday and my head hurts.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou nomisugite, atama ga itai desu
examplePolite.ja: 昨日飲みすぎて、頭が痛いです
examplePolite.english: I drank too much yesterday, so I have a headache.

items.notes: -sugi on its own is a casual exclamation: kawaisugi! (way too cute), not a mistake.
items.name: too much
items.formation: -masu stem + sugiru: tabesugiru, nomisugiru, hanashisugiru, shisugiru, kisugiru. Adjectives drop -i (takasugiru; ii → yosugiru). It then conjugates like an ichidan verb (tabesugita).

items.english: Easy to do / hard to do.
items.use: Describing things and people: kono pen kakiyasui, hanashiyasui hito. -yasui also means 'tends to': kaze hikiyasui.

example.romaji: kono kutsu, sugoku arukiyasui yo
example.ja: この靴、すごく歩きやすいよ
example.english: These shoes are really easy to walk in.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kutsu wa totemo arukiyasui desu
examplePolite.ja: この靴はとても歩きやすいです
examplePolite.english: These shoes are very easy to walk in.

items.notes: -yasui after a verb stem is 'easy to', not yasui 'cheap'.
items.name: easy / hard to do
items.formation: -masu stem + yasui or nikui: tabeyasui, kaiyasui, hanashiyasui, shiyasui, kiyasui. The result acts like an i-adjective (tabeyasukatta, wakarinikui).

blocks.label: Spoken shortcuts
blocks.rationale: Fast casual speech squeezes sounds: wakannai, -teru, -nakya, -chau. These are what make real conversation hard to follow, so each is learned as a map back to its full form.
blocks.interference: -cha (-te wa) vs -chau (-te shimau); -nakya (must) vs -nai (not); the -n of wakannai vs the n of n da.

items.english: In fast speech, -ranai and -ru before n turn into n.
items.use: All over casual speech, so you mostly need to hear it: wakannai (I don't get it), tsumannai (boring), shiran (dunno).

example.romaji: nani itteru ka zenzen wakannai
example.ja: 何言ってるか全然わかんない
example.english: I have no idea what he's saying.

items.notes: The doubled n is the whole clue: wakannai is just wakaranai, not a different word.
items.name: spoken -nnai
items.formation: Before n, a verb's r-sound becomes n: kaeranai → kaennai, wakaranai → wakannai, nani shiteru no → nani shiten no. In rough or western speech -nai can shrink to -n: shiranai → shiran.

items.english: The squeezed sounds of fast casual speech.
items.use: Nearly every casual sentence has one; learn to hear each as its full form. Using them with friends sounds natural.

example.romaji: gomen, mou kaeranakya. ashita hayai n da
example.ja: ごめん、もう帰らなきゃ。明日早いんだ
example.english: Sorry, I've got to head home. Early start tomorrow.

items.notes: -cha and -chau differ by one sound: tabecha dame = you can't eat it; tabechau = I'll eat it all up.
items.name: spoken contractions
items.formation: -nakereba → -nakya, as in the table (tabenakya, ikanakya, konakya). Also -te iru → -teru, -te oku → -toku, -te shimau → -chau, -te wa → -cha, -te iku → -teku. And de wa → ja, no da → n da, -eba → -ya (ikeba → ikya).

blocks.label: Casual emphasis
blocks.rationale: Overdo it, insist, and refuse with feeling.
blocks.interference: tteba (I said!) vs plain tte (quoting).

items.english: do like crazy; keep on doing
items.use: Attaches to the -masu stem for doing something nonstop or to excess.

example.romaji: kinou wa karaoke de utaimakutta
example.ja: 昨日はカラオケで歌いまくった
example.english: I sang my heart out at karaoke last night.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa karaoke de utaimakurimashita
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はカラオケで歌いまくりました
examplePolite.english: I sang nonstop at karaoke yesterday.

items.notes: Common with nomu, taberu, warau and kau: 'nomimakutta' (drank a ton).
items.formation: -masu stem + makuru

items.english: I said!; come on! (insisting)
items.use: Added to a repeated statement or a name when you're frustrated the other person isn't listening.

example.romaji: dakara, daijoubu da tteba!
example.ja: だから、大丈夫だってば！
example.english: I'm telling you, I'm fine!

items.notes: On a name it's an impatient call: 'okaasan tteba!' (Mom! Listen!).
items.formation: plain form or a name + tteba

items.english: as if I would!; no way
items.use: A strong, emotional refusal or denial.

example.romaji: anna yatsu ni makeru mon ka
